title: Memory Retrieval for Changing Preferences
claim: Similarity-based retrieval returns topically related but uninformative history and misses preference shifts; evidence-based retrieval finds the decisive recent turns.
layout: Single panel; timeline wave bottom, retrieval boxes top, arrow to output; sad/happy clouds
description: A single wide panel built around a wavy dashed timeline of colored dots, t1 to t_now. Each dot has a short user utterance. The utterances move from loving digital music remixes, through researching music history, losing interest, and a creativity blend, to developing tracks with nature sound recordings. The final point, t_now, is a red dot beside a user avatar and a request for something creatively fulfilling for a weekend getaway. Above the timeline are two beige boxes. On the left, Semantic emb retrieves three turns with the matched keywords in gray, and a blue cloud with a sad face says it misses the recent shift. On the right, Bayes factor retrieves nature-related turns in bold, and a blue cloud with a smiley says it locates the latest preference update. A green arrow points down to a dashed box reading 'Correctly recommends nature-soundscape adventure', next to a robot icon.
caption: Illustration of retrieval methods for personalization memory. Given a generic recommendation request, semantic embedding retrieval returns surface-similar but evidentially uninformative turns (e.g., abstract self-reflections about creativity), leading the LLM to a generic recommendation. Our Bayes Factor-based retrieval instead locates the user's recent preference shift toward nature recording, enabling the LLM to produce the correct preference-aligned recommendation.
abstract: Long-context dialogue systems must decide both when to access memory and which parts of the interaction history are relevant. Existing approaches typically rely on heuristic retrieval signals or always-on memory usage, failing to account for the changing and potentially inconsistent nature of user preferences. In this work, we propose a unified framework for memory access and selection based on changing preferences. We formulate personalized memory retrieval as identifying which historical turns provide evidence about a user's latent preference state, rather than relying on surface-level semantic similarity. To this end, we quantify the utility of each memory turn using a Bayes factor, defined as the improvement in the model's likelihood of the reference response when the turn is included in context. This provides a principled measure of evidence strength and a unified signal for both memory access and selection. By framing memory retrieval as utility estimation, the model learns to identify salient turns and regulate memory usage based on expected utility. Experiments on four heterogeneous memory benchmarks show that our approach outperforms existing embedding-based retrieval on long-context, preference-intensive tasks where modeling changing preferences is essential, while remaining competitive in low-density regimes where semantic similarity suffices.
